answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sometimes shown as microsoft.documentdb/databaseAccounts). Child resources include Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and .../collections for MongoDB API.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (az cosmosdb create, az cosmosdb update, az cosmosdb show). This is part of the core az CLI surface (no separate extension required on modern az installs). Example: az cosmosdb create -g myRG -n myAccount --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (apiVersion e.g. '2021-04-15' or newer) with properties.kind = 'MongoDB' and capabilities for serverVersion. Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account"). Configure offer_type and kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities/server_version.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical Cosmos DB MongoDB-style connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<accountname>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<accountname>@. TLS is required (ssl=true). Port is 10255 (TLS). Username/password are the MongoDB credentials (often the Cosmos account key or database user). You may also see mongodb+srv URIs for some configurations but standard form for Cosmos is host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 with ssl=true and replicaSet=globaldb.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is billed in Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput. You can provision fixed RUs or autoscale RUs; there is also a serverless option in some regions for low-throughput workloads. (The MongoDB API surface still consumes RUs; some dedicated vCore SKUs exist for other Azure DB services but Cosmos Mongo API uses RU-based billing.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API the common authentication is username/password (SCRAM-like) using Cosmos DB database users or the account keys. Cosmos account primary/secondary keys can be used to create users. Cosmos DB also supports resource tokens and role-based access control for management via Azure RBAC (Entra ID) for the control plane. Authenticating the MongoDB driver with Microsoft Entra ID (OAuth2) is not a standard flow; the MongoDB wire protocol client normally uses username/password. For management operations you use az login / Azure AD to get RBAC; for data-plane MongoDB connections use the Mongo credentials (or generated resource token in some SDKs).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For MongoDB API use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the official mongodb npm package). There is an Azure Cosmos SDK (e.g. @azure/cosmos) but that targets the SQL/core API; it is not used for the MongoDB wire API. So use the MongoDB driver and connect with the Cosmos-provided MongoDB URI.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector/indexing support on Cosmos DB Mongo API is new and vendor-specific. Expect algorithms like hnsw/IVF/DiskANN to be supported via a MongoDB-style createIndex call that specifies a vector type and algorithm. Example (approximate): db.leads.createIndex({embedding: "vector"},{name:"emb_idx", vectorOptions:{algorithm:"hnsw", dims:1536, metric:"cosine", m:16, efConstruction:200}}). Exact option names are provider-specific; this is the form I'd try to run against the cluster.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Basic text search: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})). For richer/full-text or hybrid vector+text search on Cosmos DB, use the integrated search features or pair Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search / Azure Search or use the provider's vector+text capabilities if exposed via the Mongo API (create a combined index or run a pipeline combining $text and vector similarity). In practice, many samples use Azure Cognitive Search for advanced full‑text and hybrid ranking.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports a range of MongoDB wire protocol versions; modern accounts can be set to support MongoDB 6.0/7.0 wire protocol depending on the account's serverVersion setting. However not every MongoDB server feature is supported: server-side JavaScript ($where/$eval), some aggregation stages or operators, some admin commands, and certain change stream behaviors historically are limited. Multi-shard server internals and some wire-protocol extensions may be missing. Test the exact feature surface against the account's serverVersion setting.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator but it historically supports the SQL API (and a subset of other APIs) and not always the MongoDB API. For most local dev use the official MongoDB Docker image (e.g. mongo:7) on port 27017 (mongodb://localhost:27017) to run a real MongoDB for driver-level tests. Note this will not reproduce Cosmos-specific behaviors (RUs, certain limits, vector indexes) so run integration tests against the actual Cosmos account when necessary.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Historically the MongoDB changeStream API was not fully supported on Cosmos DB Mongo API; instead Cosmos offers a Change Feed on the SQL/core API. If your account supports MongoDB wire protocol version that includes change streams you might get partial support, but you should not rely on change streams unless your account documentation explicitly lists it. In practice enable and use the Cosmos Change Feed or the provider-specific mechanism rather than relying on MongoDB change streams unless verified.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection and tooling; the general azure MCP server does not provide the same documentdb-specific commands. The sample environment mentions a 'documentdb' MCP server whose profile 'default' connects to the cluster — use that for collection/schema/index inspection and query plans.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB (a proprietary JSON document database). DocumentDB was rebranded/evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (a multi-model, globally distributed service). Azure Cosmos DB provides multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible API, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). This is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB and is not the same as AWS DocumentDB. The Cosmos MongoDB API is a compatibility layer exposing the MongoDB wire protocol on top of Cosmos storage/engine.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s Cosmos DB engine (proprietary storage/replication/consistency model) exposing a MongoDB wire protocol compatibility layer. That means applications use normal MongoDB drivers, but some server behaviors, limits, and semantics differ (throughput billed as RUs, different query planner, possible lack of some MongoDB server features). Expect subtle differences (index behaviour, aggregation support, transaction/consistency semantics) and test against the target account.

answers.question: Which database and environment variable will the sample use at runtime?
answers.answer: The sample will use the database named 'sample_customer_360_09' and read its cluster connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime (do not hard-code the URI).

answers.question: Which Node.js client and connection code will the sample use to talk to the cluster?
answers.answer: Use the official mongodb Node.js driver (npm package 'mongodb'). Connect with MongoClient using the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, {tls: true}); await client.connect(); const db = client.db('sample_customer_360_09');

answers.question: What collection and index definitions will the sample create for the lead documents and vector search?
answers.answer: Collections: 'leads' for lead documents and 'companies' for firmographics. Create a vector index on the 'leads' collection embedding field with a Mongo-style createIndex call. Example (approximate): db.leads.createIndex({embedding:'vector'},{name:'lead_emb_idx', vectorOptions:{algorithm:'hnsw',dims:1536,metric:'cosine'}}). Also create a text index for quick keyword search: db.leads.createIndex({notes:'text',title:'text'}).

answers.question: How will the agent authenticate when writing back scores to the lead document?
answers.answer: The agent will use the same MongoDB connection (DOCUMENTDB_URI credentials) and perform an authenticated update operation (collection.updateOne({_id: leadId},{$set:{score: n, scoreRationale: '...'}})). It will use the MongoDB driver's normal authentication (username/password from the connection string).

answers.question: What query pattern will the agent use to fetch signals and compute similarity?
answers.answer: Fetch activity history and engagement signals by querying leads collection by leadId and company: db.leads.findOne({_id:leadId}) and db.companies.findOne({companyId:lead.companyId}). For vector similarity run a $vectorSearch-style pipeline or use the provider vector search command, otherwise approximate by fetching top-N candidate embeddings and computing cosine similarity client-side (sort by similarity) before scoring.
